title: "Customer churn prediction in R"
output: html_document
---

```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = TRUE, warning = FALSE, message = FALSE)
```

## Objective

This notebook builds a simple customer churn prediction model using the dataset in `data.csv`.

The target variable is derived from `Buyers.Manual.scorring`:
- `B` is treated as a churn event (`1`)
- `A` is treated as a non-churn customer (`0`)
- `N/A` rows are removed from the supervised learning dataset

## 1. Load the data

```{r load-data}
df <- read.csv(
  "data.csv",
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE,
  na.strings = c("NA", "N/A", "n/a", "")
)

str(df)
```

## 2. Prepare the target and features

```{r prepare-data}
df$Buyers.Manual.scorring <- as.character(df$Buyers.Manual.scorring)
df <- df[!is.na(df$Buyers.Manual.scorring) &
           df$Buyers.Manual.scorring %in% c("A", "B"), ]

df$churn <- ifelse(df$Buyers.Manual.scorring == "B", 1, 0)

feature_cols <- setdiff(names(df), c("Vendor.ID", "Buyers.Manual.scorring", "churn"))

for (col in feature_cols) {
  df[[col]] <- suppressWarnings(as.numeric(as.character(df[[col]])))
}

df <- df[complete.cases(df[c(feature_cols, "churn")]), ]
summary(df$churn)
```

## 3. Train / test split

```{r split-data}
set.seed(42)
train_idx <- sample.int(nrow(df), size = floor(0.75 * nrow(df)))
train_df <- df[train_idx, ]
test_df  <- df[-train_idx, ]
```

## 4. Fit a logistic regression model

```{r fit-model}
model_formula <- as.formula(paste("churn ~", paste(feature_cols, collapse = " + ")))
model <- glm(model_formula, data = train_df, family = binomial())
summary(model)
```

## 5. Evaluate the model

```{r evaluate-model}
probabilities <- predict(model, newdata = test_df, type = "response")
predictions <- ifelse(probabilities >= 0.5, 1, 0)

confusion_matrix <- table(Actual = test_df$churn, Predicted = predictions)
print(confusion_matrix)

accuracy <- mean(predictions == test_df$churn)
precision <- sum(predictions == 1 & test_df$churn == 1) / max(sum(predictions == 1), 1)
recall <- sum(predictions == 1 & test_df$churn == 1) / max(sum(test_df$churn == 1), 1)

cat(sprintf("Accuracy: %.3f\n", accuracy))
cat(sprintf("Precision: %.3f\n", precision))
cat(sprintf("Recall: %.3f\n", recall))

positive_scores <- probabilities[test_df$churn == 1]
negative_scores <- probabilities[test_df$churn == 0]

if (length(positive_scores) > 0 && length(negative_scores) > 0) {
  rank_sum <- sum(rank(c(positive_scores, negative_scores))[seq_along(positive_scores)])
  auc <- (rank_sum - length(positive_scores) * (length(positive_scores) + 1) / 2) /
    (length(positive_scores) * length(negative_scores))
  cat(sprintf("AUC: %.3f\n", auc))
} else {
  cat("AUC could not be computed because the test set is missing one class.\n")
}
```

## 6. Review the most important variables

```{r variable-importance}
coefficients <- coef(model)
print(coefficients[order(abs(coefficients), decreasing = TRUE)])
```

## Interpretation

This is a simple baseline model intended to demonstrate the churn-prediction workflow. In practice, it can be improved with:

- better churn labeling
- class balancing
- cross-validation
- feature engineering
- comparison with random forest, gradient boosting, or XGBoost
